children.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do
children.blurb: In the fall of 2023, nearly 1,000 students at a high school in Turkey took part in a simple test. During math review sessions, some students practiced with a plain AI chat tool, much like the free chatbots anyone can open on a phone.

children.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere
children.blurb: When this Volume began, the raw material was a stack of 1,200 ideas for using AI in schools, gathered from teachers, district leaders, researchers, and product lists. Reading them one by one felt like walking through a crowded market where every stall sold something slightly different.

children.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule
children.blurb: In June 2026, a school board member in Portland, Oregon, raised concerns about the data an AI reading assessment company would collect from students. The list of data fields in the company's contract included items such as place of birth and migrant status (Willamette Week, 2026).

children.name: Pilot, Measure, Scale
children.blurb: In a recent trial in Germany, 371 students in grades 7 through 9 used generative AI tools during six regular physics and English lessons. Some students got a tool designed to build motivation, some got a tool designed to teach learning strategies, and a comparison group used a plain chatbot.

sections.body: Getting Oriented is the opening part of the book's treatment of AI in education, and it sets the foundation for everything that comes after. It explains what AI can and cannot do, the ten patterns that account for nearly every idea in the Volume, the laws and rules that protect students, and a simple method for piloting and measuring any new tool. In this part of school life, AI is not yet being applied to a subject or a classroom task. Instead, the book is describing the ground rules and the basic understanding a reader needs before any tool is used with students.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book holds that readers who start nowhere else should start here, because the rules set out in these chapters apply to every idea in the chapters that follow. What works is beginning with a clear account of AI's limits, the recurring patterns, the legal protections for students, and a disciplined way to try and measure a tool. What does not work is skipping this grounding and moving straight to tools or lessons. The rule the book holds to is that the foundation comes first, and the protections and the pilot method carry forward into everything else.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages fit together as a sequence from understanding to protection to practice. What AI Can and Cannot Do gives the teacher or leader the plain account of the technology's limits, and Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere gives the recurring ideas that reappear throughout the Volume. Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule is where a leader or parent turns for the laws and rules that protect students and for the human review requirement. Pilot, Measure, Scale is the practical method a teacher or leader uses to try any new tool and judge whether it should grow, and it depends on the earlier pages because the rules they set out apply to every idea that follows.
